note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: Sudden inability to move left arm upon waking approximately 1 hour prior to call.
- Symptom onset: Acute, occurred on waking this morning.
- Duration: ~1 hour.
- Progression: Persistent inability to move left arm; speech and swallowing have become more difficult during the call.
- Associated symptoms: Tingling on left side of face since onset, mild facial droop when attempting to drink, some swallowing difficulties, speech feels slower and more effortful; denies facial asymmetry on observation, no pain, no limb discoloration or temperature changes, no symptoms in left leg. 
- No previous episodes reported. No known recent trauma or unusual sleeping position.
- Social: Lives alone. Previously smoked; current alcohol intake includes several pints of beer per week.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes
- Hypertension
- Allergies: Penicillin
- Medications: Metformin, Losartan, Amlodipine (dose/route/frequency not documented)
- Family history: Father with heart disease (details unclear)

Physical Examination:
- Unable to move left arm (self-reported)
- No pain in affected limb
- No discoloration or coldness of left hand/arm
- Tingling on left side of face
- Mild difficulty when drinking (possible subtle facial weakness)
- Swallowing difficulty reported
- Speech slower and more effortful than baseline
- No symptoms in left leg
- No apparent facial asymmetry by patient report
- Alert and able to converse on phone

Impression:
- Acute left-sided hemiparesis, facial symptoms, and speech/swallowing difficulty—suspicious for acute cerebrovascular event (stroke).

Management Plan:
- Emergency ambulance called for immediate transfer to hospital (A&E).
- Patient instructed to leave front door unlocked and sit in hallway for rapid access by paramedics.
- Doctor to remain on phone with patient until ambulance arrives.
- Advise no further activity until paramedics arrive.

Patient Summary:
- Jack Armani presented with sudden-onset left arm paralysis, facial tingling, swallowing and speech difficulties on awakening. Symptoms are ongoing and worsening, consistent with possible acute stroke. Emergency services have been called for immediate evaluation and treatment.

Key Takeaways:
- Acute neurological symptoms require urgent hospital assessment.
- Patient must not eat, drink, or exert themselves before paramedic evaluation.
- Ensure immediate access for emergency services.

Next Steps:
- Hospital-based stroke assessment and management to be initiated on arrival (e.g., imaging, possible thrombolysis per hospital protocol).
- Monitor for progression of neurological deficits en route.
- Further investigation of risk factors (e.g., blood pressure, blood glucose) to be done in hospital.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):

● Missing but clinically expected elements: 
  - Full medication reconciliation (dose/route/frequency not collected)
  - No vital signs, physical exam findings are self-reported, no in-person neuro assessment possible
  - No detailed allergy history beyond penicillin
  - No past surgical or hospitalization history
  - No recent labs, imaging, or prior functional baseline documented
● Internal conflicts: None evident from transcript.
● Transcript quality: Clear; minor repetitions, but clinically relevant details well covered. No significant noise or inaudible sections.
